Using Resources.intro: Humans use the Earth's resources to make materials and products. Understanding sustainable use of resources is crucial for C10.

sections.title: Natural and Synthetic Materials
points: Natural resources: extracted from Earth — metals, wood, cotton, limestone
Synthetic materials: made from natural resources through chemical processes — plastics, medicines, alloys
Finite resources: will run out — fossil fuels, metals
Renewable resources: can be replenished — wood, crops, solar energy

sections.title: Sustainable Development

callout.label: Definition
callout.text: Sustainable development meets the needs of the current generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

points: Reduce, reuse, recycle — conserves finite resources
Use renewable energy sources
Develop more efficient processes
Life cycle assessment (LCA) helps evaluate environmental impact

keyTerms.def: A resource that will eventually run out — cannot be replenished
A resource that can be replenished naturally
Development that meets current needs without compromising future generations

examTips: Metals are finite — they must be mined; recycling conserves them.
Know the sustainable development definition — it often comes up in 6-mark questions.
commonMistakes: Saying wood is a finite resource — it is renewable if managed sustainably.
Confusing reusing (same purpose) with recycling (reprocessed into new material).

Life Cycle Assessment.intro: A life cycle assessment (LCA) evaluates the environmental impact of a product from raw material extraction to disposal.

sections.title: What LCA Considers
points: Energy use at each stage
Water use
Carbon footprint (CO₂ emissions)
Waste and pollution generated
Resource depletion

callout.label: Limitations
callout.text: LCAs can be subjective — different companies may weigh factors differently. Can be used selectively to support a commercial argument. Numerical data may be incomplete.

keyTerms.def: An evaluation of the environmental impact of a product throughout its entire life
Total CO₂ (and equivalent) emissions from a product or process

examTips: LCA covers the WHOLE life of a product — from raw materials to disposal.
Be critical of LCAs — they can be biased and involve value judgements.
commonMistakes: Saying LCAs are completely objective — they involve subjective judgements about what to measure.
Forgetting disposal stage — many students only consider manufacturing.

Water.intro: Water is essential for life and industry. Understanding how water is made safe to drink and the difference between potable and pure water is required for C10.

sections.title: Potable Water
points: Potable = safe to drink (not the same as chemically pure)
Contains dissolved salts and minerals — not 100% pure H₂O
UK sources: surface water (rivers, lakes), ground water (aquifers)

sections.title: Making Water Potable
numbered: Filtration — sand and gravel filters remove smaller particles
Chlorination — chlorine added to kill microorganisms

sections.title: Desalination
points: Removes salt from seawater — used in water-scarce countries
Methods: distillation (energy intensive) or reverse osmosis (uses high pressure)
Expensive and high energy use — not widely used in UK

keyTerms.def: Water that is safe to drink — not necessarily pure
The removal of dissolved salts from seawater to make it drinkable
Adding chlorine to water to kill microorganisms

examTips: Potable ≠ pure. Potable water contains dissolved substances but is safe to drink.
Chlorination kills microorganisms — does not remove dissolved salts.
commonMistakes: Saying potable water is pure water — potable means safe to drink, not chemically pure.
Confusing filtration (removes particles) with chlorination (kills microbes).

Alternative Metal Extraction.intro: Traditional metal extraction uses carbon reduction or electrolysis, but newer methods are being developed for low-grade ores and environmental reasons.

sections.title: Traditional Extraction
points: Metals below carbon in reactivity series: reduced by carbon (e.g. iron in blast furnace)
Metals above carbon (e.g. aluminium): extracted by electrolysis (more expensive)
Mining has environmental impact: habitat destruction, pollution

sections.title: Phytomining
points: Plants absorb metal compounds through roots
Plants are harvested and burned
Ash contains metal compounds — processed to extract metal
Useful for low-grade ores not worth traditional mining

sections.title: Bioleaching
points: Bacteria break down low-grade metal ores
Produce an acidic solution (leachate) containing metal ions
Metal extracted from solution by electrolysis or displacement
Slower than traditional methods but lower environmental impact

keyTerms.def: Using plants to absorb metal compounds from soil, then burning to extract the metal
Using bacteria to extract metals from low-grade ores
Rock containing only a small percentage of the desired metal

examTips: Phytomining = plants absorb metal → burn → extract from ash.
Bioleaching = bacteria produce acidic solution containing metal ions.
Both are useful for low-grade ores where traditional extraction is uneconomical.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the final step — metal still needs extracting from the solution/ash.

Corrosion.intro: Corrosion is the degradation of metals by reaction with their environment. Rusting is the most common example.

sections.title: Rusting
points: Iron reacts with oxygen AND water to form hydrated iron(III) oxide (rust)
Both oxygen and water are needed — neither alone causes rust
Rust is a redox reaction — iron is oxidised

sections.title: Prevention
points: Painting or oiling — creates barrier preventing water and oxygen contact
Galvanising — coating with zinc; zinc is sacrificial (more reactive, oxidises first)
Electroplating — coating with another metal (e.g. chromium for stainless steel appearance)
Sacrificial protection — attach more reactive metal (zinc/magnesium); it corrodes instead

keyTerms.def: Degradation of a metal by reaction with its environment
Oxidation of iron in the presence of water and oxygen
Coating iron with zinc to prevent rusting
Attaching a more reactive metal that corrodes instead of the protected metal

examTips: Rusting needs BOTH oxygen AND water — remove either to prevent it.
Galvanising works by both barrier AND sacrificial protection — zinc is more reactive than iron.
commonMistakes: Saying only oxygen causes rust — water is also needed.
Forgetting that galvanising works by sacrificial protection even if the zinc coating is scratched.

Materials.intro: Different materials have different properties making them suitable for different uses. Understanding how structure determines properties is key to materials science.

sections.title: Ceramics
points: Made from clay, heated to high temperatures
Hard, brittle, high melting point, good thermal and electrical insulators
Examples: glass, pottery, brick, cement

sections.title: Composites
points: Made from two or more materials combined — matrix and reinforcement
Properties combine benefits of both components
Examples: carbon fibre reinforced polymer (CFRP) — light and strong
Concrete = aggregate + cement (composite); fibreglass = glass fibres + polymer

sections.title: Glass and Clay
points: Soda-lime glass: made from sand (SiO₂), limestone, sodium carbonate — common glass
Borosilicate glass: more heat-resistant — lab glassware
Glass-ceramic: can withstand thermal shock — hob cooktops

keyTerms.def: Hard, brittle material made from clay fired at high temperature
Material made from two or more materials combined to have improved properties
Long-chain molecule; many synthetic polymers used as materials (plastics)

examTips: Composites combine properties of their components — explain what each component contributes.
Ceramics are brittle — they crack rather than deform under stress.
commonMistakes: Confusing composites (two materials combined) with alloys (two metals mixed).
Forgetting that glass is a ceramic — it's made from silicon dioxide.
